meta.title: Who really said "History is but a fable agreed upon"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The words are in Voltaire — but spoken by a character he is mocking, who himself credits 'one of our wits.' The idea traces to Fontenelle (1724); the famous English epigram came via Napoleon. The 'lies agreed upon' version is not Voltaire at all.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'History is but a fable agreed upon'?
meta.ogDescription: It appears in Voltaire's Jeannot et Colin (1764) — in the mouth of a fashionable fool he is satirising, who attributes it to someone else. Not Voltaire's view, and not his coinage.

answer.label: The words are in Voltaire — but they are not his view
answer.sourceLine: The line does appear in Voltaire — in the tale Jeannot et Colin (1764): “Toutes les histoires anciennes… ne sont que des fables convenues.” But it is spoken by a fashionable homme d’esprit hired to advise on a boy’s education, who uses it to argue that history need not be studied at all — and Voltaire is mocking him. The character even credits the line to “one of our wits.” So it is quoted from a satire, in the wrong voice, and it was not original there either.

source.excerpt: Toutes les histoires anciennes… ne sont que des fables convenues.
trail: The French is in Jeannot et Colin (1764). The English of the standard public-domain translation runs: ‘all ancient histories, as one of our wits has observed, are only fables that men have agreed to admit as true’ — note that the speaker is himself quoting somebody else the tale ↗.

The idea predates the tale: Fontenelle’s De l’Origine des Fables (1724) argues that ancient histories are essentially fables, and Helvétius credited Fontenelle with the sentiment in 1758 Quote Investigator ↗.

The compact English epigram entered circulation through Napoleon, who used it at St Helena in 1816 — and explicitly disclaimed originating it. Emerson then credited Napoleon in his essay ‘History’ (1841), which is how English readers met it full chain ↗.
source.excerptNote: The French as Voltaire wrote it — in a character’s mouth. The one-line English epigram people quote is a later compression that strips both the speaker and his own attribution.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: About Voltaire
author.bio: Voltaire — pen name of François-Marie Arouet — was the wit and conscience of the French Enlightenment. He was also a serious historian, author of Le Siècle de Louis XIV, who argued for evidence and against credulity in the writing of history. That is the irony here: a line dismissing history as fiction is quoted as his creed, when in his own tale it belongs to a shallow fashionable adviser he is holding up for ridicule.

misattribution.heading: Right book, wrong voice
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quotation — you can find it in Voltaire. It is something subtler and more common than a fake: a line lifted out of a satire and reported as the author’s own opinion.

items.why: The words belong to a fashionable adviser in Jeannot et Colin who is arguing that a boy need not learn history. Voltaire — a working historian — is ridiculing him. Quoting it as Voltaire’s view inverts the passage the tale ↗.
Even inside the story the character presents it as somebody else’s line. The idea itself goes back at least to Fontenelle in 1724 the chain ↗.

‘History is a set of lies agreed upon’ has no Voltaire basis. It is a hardening of Napoleon’s form, and the ‘lies’ wording traces to Wendell Phillips in 1881. Do not credit that one to Voltaire under any circumstances.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely in Voltaire’s Jeannot et Colin (1764) — spoken by a character he is satirising, who credits an unnamed wit. The idea is Fontenelle’s; the epigram is Napoleon’s full trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the most quotable form of a real suspicion — that the past we are handed has been tidied by whoever did the handing. Attached to Voltaire, the arch-skeptic, it reads as Enlightenment realism about power and record-keeping.

In the tale it does the opposite work. The man who says it is a fool using cynicism as an excuse for ignorance, and Voltaire — who spent years in archives writing history himself — is showing you exactly that.
detailsBody: Fontenelle, De l’Origine des Fables (1724): ancient histories are essentially fables.
Voltaire, Jeannot et Colin (1764): a satirised character says ‘fables convenues,’ crediting ‘one of our wits.’
Napoleon, St Helena (1816): ‘What then is the truth of history? A fable agreed upon’ — and he disclaimed inventing it.
Emerson, ‘History’ (1841): credits Napoleon, carrying the epigram into English.
Wendell Phillips (1881): ‘a series of lies agreed upon’ — the source of the ‘lies’ variant.
context.pull: Voltaire wrote the line for a fool. We quote it as his creed.
